name: old cracked asphalt road of cool charcoal grey with fine scattered non-directional aggregate specks, faded slightly warmer patches, thin crack lines, soft stains and worn broken fragments of yellow and white lane paint, its unconnected edges broken off into dirt as a chipped asphalt lip with loose asphalt chunks, laid as a road network with crossroads and dead ends
label: wasteland_ruins/asphalt

surfaces.part: asphalt road patches on dirt ground (flat terrain tile)

answer.evidence: This is a terrain autotile sheet. A flat dirt ground fills the full 256x192 area, with road pieces (a crossroads, dead ends, a corner, a small patch and a large block) drawn as flat top-down grey asphalt. The edges show only a thin dark chipped lip of 1-2 rows. No vertical front face of 3 or more rows is drawn, and there is no standing volume. It reads as a flat top-down ground surface, which is normal for terrain, so the kind matches.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has about 5 visible tones per tile, which is in the range of the paving reference (7) and above the grass reference (3). Near-flat coverage is 5%, and its dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outlines are tinted rather than black. The picture shows a different story. The asphalt itself is a shallow ramp of about 3 greys, a dark charcoal base with a few lighter speckles, where the paving reference shows 5-6 stepped tones with per-stone highlights. The road shapes are small and sparse. The dirt background takes up most of the patch, so the asphalt carries little of the information. The lane paint is a single yellow fleck, and the white paint is missing. The cracks are thin and few, and the warm patches and stains are barely visible. The chipped lip is mostly a uniform dark edge, without the loose chunks the brief asks for. Overall it is cleaner and flatter than the Beodeul quality bar, and a careful artist would see it as thinner than the reference.

surfaces.part: asphalt road patches on dirt ground (flat terrain tileset)

answer.evidence: This is a flat terrain tileset viewed straight down: grey asphalt road shapes (crossroads, dead ends, a large block) on a brown dirt background. There is no standing volume. The chipped edges have only a thin dark 1-row lip along the bottom of some shapes, which reads as an edge shadow, not a front face of 3 or more rows. The column scan shows only dirt speckle and crack runs, with no top band, front-edge line or front face. Terrain tiles are judged as flat ground, so there is no top surface or front face to measure.

styleAnswer.evidence: The asphalt reads as 2-3 steps: a mid charcoal with darker specks and a dark edge, against about 6 for the paving reference. The candidate has only 14 distinct colours, and about 5 visible tones per tile compared with 7 for paving and 3 for grass, so density is not far off the references, but the asphalt itself is shallow. The asphalt patches are small and blobby. The road network is thin and sparse, with chunky chipped edges, and the big charcoal pieces are mostly flat grey with only light speckle. The lane paint is a single tiny yellow dash, so the worn white and yellow paint is barely there, and cracks are few. The dirt ground takes up most of the board and has some speckle, but it is a single mid-brown ramp of 3-4 tones. Edge pixels are tinted rather than neutral (0% neutral), but the dark rim on the asphalt is a uniform dark grey outline around every blob, which looks like a sticker. Compared with the paving reference, which has per-stone shading and highlights, the candidate looks thinner and flatter. The candidate also lacks a clear 4x3 tiled layout with proper crossroads and dead ends, and the shapes are scattered, disconnected blobs.

styleAnswer.evidence: The asphalt reads as 3 lightness steps (dark charcoal, mid grey, a few lighter specks) against the references' 5-6. The 14 distinct colours and 5 visible tones per tile are low next to the paving reference (7 tones) but above the grass (3). The dirt ground is mottled with brown speckle and has no big flat areas (5% near-flat). The asphalt patches are small, sparse blobs. Their edges are a darker grey that leans slightly neutral and are not clearly a tinted material tone, so I call the outline mixed. The shapes look like stamped-on sticker blobs, not a road network with real crossroads. The crack lines and the single yellow paint fleck are thin and sparse. The asphalt lacks the per-stone shading and highlight clusters the paving reference has. It is shallower than a Beodeul piece.

surfaces.part: asphalt road patches on dirt ground (flat terrain tile)

answer.evidence: This is a terrain tileset: a full-width 256x192 sheet of brown dirt with grey asphalt road pieces (crossroads, dead ends, a large block). The roads are flat ground surfaces seen from above. Each piece has a thin dark chipped lip along its south edge, but that is only an edge line with no vertical front face of 3+ rows. The column scans show only dirt-colour runs with small dark crack or lip rows. Because it is terrain rather than a standing object, no top surface or front face applies, so it reads as a flat top-down surface.

styleAnswer.evidence: The asphalt pieces are small, flat-looking grey blobs on a brown dirt field. The asphalt ramp shows only about 3 steps (dark grey, mid grey, a slightly lighter speck) against the paving reference's 6-7. Measured visible tones per tile are 5, below the paving reference's 7 and above the grass reference's 3. Near-flat coverage is 5%, which is low but not zero. The dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outlines lean tinted rather than black. The asphalt lacks the per-stone shading and highlight clusters of the paving reference, and the cracks and lane paint are sparse: one small yellow mark, with no visible white paint. The edge chips are blocky and uniform. The dirt carries only 2-3 brown tones of speckle. Raw distinct colours total only 14 against the references' 80 and 7 per tile, so the whole patch is shallow in shading steps and reads as a sticker-like cutout against the references. A careful artist would not accept it next to the paving reference without it looking flatter.
